blocks.text: An interval is just a range with a start and an end, like a meeting from 2pm to 3pm, or the numbers from 5 to 9. Simple as that sounds, intervals power a whole family of classic interview problems.

Booking calendars, scheduling meeting rooms, merging overlapping time ranges, and finding free slots are all interval problems in disguise. Once you learn the handful of core ideas here, a large group of problems suddenly feels familiar.
The interval pattern is really about one question asked in many ways: how do these ranges relate to each other? Do they overlap, touch, or sit apart?
An interval is a pair of values, a start and an end, that marks a continuous range. Everything between the two endpoints belongs to the interval.

blocks.alt: An interval spans from a start to an end: [start, end]

blocks.text: For example, the interval from 2 to 5 covers 2, 3, 4, and 5. A meeting from 9 to 10 occupies that whole hour. The two numbers are all you need to describe the range.

items: Everything in between is part of the interval.

blocks.text: In code, an interval is usually a small pair or list holding the start and the end. A collection of intervals is then a list of these pairs.

codes.python:
interval = [2, 5]              # one interval from 2 to 5

intervals = [[1, 3], [6, 9], [2, 4]]   # a list of intervals

blocks.text: The first number is the start and the second is the end. Almost every interval problem hands you a list like this and asks you to reason about how the ranges overlap.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406552912-622646998.png
This single idea is the heart of the entire pattern. Two intervals overlap when they share at least one point. Getting this check right unlocks almost everything else.
The clean rule: intervals A and B overlap when A starts before or when B ends, and B starts before or when A ends.

codes.python:
def overlaps(a, b):
    return a[0] <= b[1] and b[0] <= a[1]

print(overlaps([1, 5], [4, 8]))   # True, they share 4 and 5
print(overlaps([1, 3], [6, 9]))   # False, a gap between them

blocks.text: It is often easier to think about when intervals do NOT overlap: one ends completely before the other begins. Everything else is an overlap.
Almost every interval problem begins the same way: sort the intervals, usually by their start value. This one step turns a tangled mess into a clean left to right order.
Once sorted, you can walk through the intervals in order and only ever compare each one with the previous result. You never have to look backward or compare every pair.

codes.python: intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])   # sort by start value

blocks.text: If you feel stuck on an interval problem, sort by start first. Nine times out of ten, that is the move that makes the solution appear.
This is the flagship interval problem, and it appears constantly. You are given a list of intervals, some of which overlap, and you must combine the overlapping ones into single ranges.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406552914-395425192.png
The approach: sort by start, then walk through. If the current interval overlaps the last one in your result, stretch that last one. Otherwise, start a new interval.
After sorting, overlapping intervals sit next to each other, so a single pass is enough. This runs in the time it takes to sort, which is O(n log n).
A close cousin: you have a list of sorted, non overlapping intervals and you must insert a new one, merging it with any it overlaps.
You walk through in three phases: add all intervals that end before the new one starts, merge everything that overlaps the new one, then add the rest.

codes.python:
def insert(intervals, new):
    result = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    # intervals entirely before the new one
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new[0]:
        result.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    # merge all that overlap the new one
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new[1]:
        new[0] = min(new[0], intervals[i][0])
        new[1] = max(new[1], intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append(new)
    # intervals entirely after
    while i < n:
        result.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    return result

blocks.text: A common simpler question: given a list of meetings, can one person attend all of them, or do any of them clash?
Sort by start, then check each interval against the previous one. If any interval starts before the previous one ended, there is a clash.
This is the well known Meeting Rooms problem. After sorting, you only ever compare neighbours, which is why sorting is so powerful here.
A deeper question: at the busiest moment, how many intervals overlap? This tells you, for example, how many meeting rooms you need so no meeting is left without a room.
The trick is to look at starts and ends as separate events on a timeline. A start adds one to the count, an end removes one. The highest the count ever reaches is your answer.
This idea is so important that it has its own name, the line sweep, and its own lesson right after this one.
Sometimes you want the parts that two lists of intervals share in common, meaning where they overlap. This is interval intersection.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406552915-301568951.png
Walk both lists together with two pointers. For each pair, the overlap, if any, runs from the larger of the two starts to the smaller of the two ends.
Most interval problems are variations of a few core tasks. Recognising which one you are facing points you straight at the solution.

items: Merge: combine overlapping ranges into single ones.
Insert: add a range and merge what it touches.
Clash detection: can all meetings be attended without overlap?
Max overlap: how many overlap at the busiest point, meaning rooms needed.
Intersection: the shared parts of two lists of ranges.
Free slots: the gaps left between busy intervals.

blocks.text: Almost every interval question is one of these wearing a story. Meeting rooms, calendars, and CPU jobs are the same problems dressed differently.
The cost of interval problems is dominated by the sorting step at the start.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Cost"],"rows":[["Sorting the intervals","O(n log n)"],["The single pass afterwards","O(n)"],["Overall","O(n log n)"]]}

blocks.text: The sort is the expensive part. The clever walk that follows is only a single linear pass, which is why these solutions are so efficient once sorted.

items: Forgetting to sort first, which makes the neighbour comparisons meaningless
Getting the overlap check wrong, especially at the exact touching endpoints
Deciding whether ranges that only touch at a point count as overlapping
Mutating the input list when the problem expects it untouched
Comparing every pair of intervals, which is slow, instead of only neighbours after sorting

blocks.text: Always clarify whether touching endpoints count as an overlap, for example whether an interval ending at 5 clashes with one starting at 5. The answer changes your comparison.
Should I sort by start or by end?
Sort by start for most problems like merging and clash detection. A few problems, such as choosing the most non overlapping intervals, sort by end instead. When in doubt, start with the start.
Do intervals that touch count as overlapping?
It depends on the problem. An interval ending at 5 and one starting at 5 may or may not clash, so always confirm the rule before coding the comparison.
Why is sorting always the first step?
Because once intervals are in order by start, overlaps only ever happen between neighbours, so a single pass solves the problem instead of comparing every pair.
What is the connection to line sweep?
Line sweep is the technique for counting how many intervals overlap at once, by treating starts and ends as events on a timeline. It is the next lesson.
These problems are the classic way to lock in the interval pattern.

items: Merge a list of overlapping intervals into the fewest ranges.
Insert a new interval into a sorted list and merge overlaps.
Decide whether a person can attend all their meetings.
Find the intersection of two lists of intervals.
Find the free gaps left between a set of busy intervals.

blocks.text: Master merging and the overlap check first. Almost every other interval problem builds directly on those two ideas. Then move on to line sweep for the counting problems.
